nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Tarpon
Scientific Name: Megalops atlanticus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Elopiformes
	Family:  Elopidae


Other Common Names: tarpum(310 749 846); caffum(310 749); sabalo real, palika(310); sabalo (846 1364); silverfish(310 312 834 846 1364);  silver king(310 327 749); jewfish(310 312 1364); big scale(1364); grande ecaille(255 310 327 846 1364); grand ecoy(255 1364); sadina (1364); savalle, savanilla(846 1364); king fish(834)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  No commercial value in United States where it is considered inedible (312 834 846 858 749 1364), but considered a delicacy in Panama, West Indies, and Africa, where it is sold on a small scale (66 310 749).  A commercial fishery exists in Colombia (791).  Caught mainly on hook and line, but also with dynamite in the southern Caribbean (791).  Flesh is rather fatty, but it is marketed fresh or salted (791 846).  Scales used in ornamental work and for the preparation of artificial pearls (312 791 834 846).

Recreational: Excellent game fish sought for sporting purposes throughout most of its range.  Well known for fighting ability and aerial acrobatics, it is commonly regarded as a prime inshore game fish (310 312 664 749 788 834 846 858 1364).  No size limit in Florida, but there is a 2 fish bag limit and a tarpon tag costing $50 is required to possess or kill.

Indicator:  Dieldrin, a chlorinated hydrocarbon used for mosquito control, has been shown to cause mortality to tarpon (750 1365 1366).  Tarpon are also considered natural monitors of toxic pollutants in inshore areas because of their freedom from reliance on dissolved oxygen for survival where, by contrast, oxygen depletion cannot be ruled out at the immediate cause of death of other species (278).

Ecological Role: Tarpon are high trophic level carnivores preying mainly on fish (750).  Due to the large relative size of tarpon juveniles these fish undoubtedly shape the population structure of other species in habitats including wetland mosquito impoundments.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  In the western Atlantic from Nova Scotia, where it rarely occurs in the summer, to central Brazil and throughout the Gulf of Mexico and the West Indies (310 312 327 749 788 791 891 1037). Also reported at the Pacific terminus of the Panama Canal (749).  Occurrences from the Carolinas northward are sparse, and it appears only as a straggler north of the Carolinas (278 310 312 327 749 750 834).  Centers of abundance are the Gulf of Mexico, coastal Florida, and the West Indies (205 310 659 791 858).  In the eastern Atlantic from Ireland to the Congo with reports from Bermuda, the Azores, and the Formigas (738 749 750 791),  Center of abundance is from Senegal to the Congo (750).  Chief center of abundance is in the western Atlantic (750).

Within Study Area:  Found throughout Florida coastal waters (310 749 848 858 891).  Highly abundant on both the east and west coasts of Florida especially at Boca Grande and Captiva, western Florida; the waterways and rivers of the Thousand Islands, and the interior waterways of the Florida Keys (310 790).  Most abundant in the Tampa Bay area from spring through fall (664).

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Non-schooling but does form congregations while feeding (278 310 1037).  No information is available on eggs; early larval forms are pelagic and planktonic, while later larval stages, juveniles, and adults are pelagic and nektonic (231 659).  Some evidence of increased larval activity at night (735) while adults feed both day and night (749).

Spatial Strategy:  Larva1: (leptocephalus): Warm, western Atlantic epipelagic waters north of the equator with all recoveries occurring in the upper 100 m of water (749 1365) in euhaline salinities as far out as 240 km and to depths of 200 m (231 659 749 1372); also collected from inshore waters (198 1367).

Larva2:  (shrinking): Recorded from depths of <1 to 12 m in inshore waters (201 706 735). Collected in salt marshes, rivers, mangrove swamps, estuaries, and upper reaches of bays as far north as Cape Fear River, North Carolina (66 201 278 280 706 735 749) in mesohaline to euhaline waters (706 735 749).

Larva3: (growing): Found along beaches in lagoons, salt marshes, ponds, potholes, rivers and canals (280 310 366 749 1368); rarely collected as far north as North Carolina (1369).

Juvenile:  Smaller individuals found in shallow streams, lakes, marshes, lagoons, ponds, ditches, canals, rivers, estuaries, mangrove swamps, pools, and drainage ditches nearly or completely landlocked except for periods of extreme high water; also in headwaters of small freshwater streams (66 280 299 310 327 344 442 515 579 596 703 749 750).  Usually in dark colored brackish waters, stagnant or flowing (579 596 749) in depths of 15.2 to 152.4 cm (224 579 596 656 750).  Tarpon 305_487 mm common in headwaters of brackish and freshwater streams.  Movement to deeper rivers, canals, pools, lakes, and eventually to ocean occurs as individuals grow larger (310 750) being found in waters 0.9 to 2.5 m deep (224 255 596 702 750).  Juvenile tarpon are the largest predator utilizing wetland impoundments along the IRL (1272).

Adults: Primarily in coastal inshore waters, inlets, estuaries, and passes between islands, but also found in deeper rivers canals, streams, and lakes (66 310 327 395 749 750 788 791 848) in freshwater to marine environments (66 395 579 703 749 788 790 1365).

Movements and Migrations:  Observations suggest that tarpon larvae may move to offshore waters from spawning areas returning to inshore areas prior to metamorphosis (201 231 281 659).  As juvenile tarpon grow, they move from nursery grounds to deeper inshore waters and finally to the ocean (750).  Adult and large juvenile tarpon are capable of extensive movements, but patterns of coastal migration other than inshore-offshore movements in response to the cooling waters of winter are not evident (310 481 579), although some individuals apparently move northward along the Atlantic coast during the summer and are subsequently lost to the population (310).  Tarpon are most abundant inshore from April to November (69 320 668).  Assemblages of sexually maturing tarpon observed during spring and summer may by preparatory to an offshore spawning migration (481).

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body: Juveniles and adults generally found over soft mud bottoms sometimes containing H2S, but also over sand, firm mud, sandy mud with no vegetation, peat (224 255 579 596 656 703 702 750), and occasionally on coral reefs (788).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Eggs: No information

Larva1:  larvae occur only in warm oceanic waters ranging from 22.2 to 30.0 C (659 749).  They appear to prefer warmer waters (366).  Stage II larvae reported from 19.8  to 30.8 C (706 735).  Larva3: reported from 25.0 to 27.0 C (278).

Juveniles/Adults: Range and habitat essentially the same for both groups (749); they have been collected at temperatures ranging from 12.0 to 40.0 C (224 235 255 442 514 579 596 656 702 750 1375).  In Florida, juveniles have been collected at temperatures of 23.0 to 33.0 C at Naples and 17.0 to 37.0 C near Indian River (1374).  Loss of equilibrium or death observed from 9.5 to 18.2 C in the laboratory (344).  Mortality occurs in the wild at temperatures between 10.0 and 14.0 C following sudden cold snaps (596).  One dead specimen was found at Tampa Bay when water temperature was 13.0 C (664).  Resistance to cold might be greater during slow temperature falls (596 702).  Listed as one of the species killed by freezes at Sanibel Island, Florida (836 1068).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Eggs: No information

Larva1: Specimens taken from 28.5 to 39.0 ppt (198 659 749 1370 1371).  Possibly stenohaline, seeming to prefer high salinities as this stage is not generally found in low or fluctuating salinities, probably staying well offshore until the approach of metamorphosis (659).

Larva2/Larva3/Juvenile/Adult:  Euryhaline; collected at salinities ranging from 0.0 to 47 ppt, but seem to prefer salinities between 5.1 and 22.3 ppt (66 224 255 261 278 395 442 514 579 596 651 656 702 706 735 750).  Widely distributed in the freshwaters of south Florida where they are primarily restricted to deep water (790).  Found in freshwater canals throughout the Everglades, the Big Cypress Swamp and along both coasts (395). Also found in Lake Okeechobee (1313).

Dissolved oxygen: Tarpon are obligate air breathers (749) with metamorphosing larvae as small as 16 mm SL dying if kept from surfacing as do larger fish (278).  Juveniles may occupy areas of low DO as a way to avoid predators because many predators cannot tolerate anoxic waters (278 749).  Juvenile growth may be retarded by continued occupation of anoxic waters (1374).  Tarpon are able to breathe by means of rolling and gulping air which is held in a highly vascularized air bladder (514 750).  Their ability for aerial respiration allows them to survive in oxygen depleted waters with an oxygen content as low as 0.00 to 0.81 ppm (514).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Sexes separate; probably external fertilization

Mating/Spawning: Unknown; apparently restricted to offshore waters such as east coast of Florida to Cape Hatteras, Florida Straits, west central Florida, southwestern Gulf of Mexico, Gulf Stream, and Caribbean Sea, or areas where currents can carry eggs offshore, possibly in shoal waters between coastal islands, or close to shore in salty or brackish water (66 198 281 310 366 659 750 1370).  Some populations may complete life cycle in fresh water (310).  Estimated spawning season is from May to September with near ripe females and milt ejecting males occurring in April and spent females occurring in July and August (66 198 310 366 579 659 750 1365).  Cyr (1374) examined reproductive condition of tarpon from Boca Grande, Tampa Bay and other south Florida areas. He found that the peak in reproductive development occurred in May and June with the greatest number of spent males and females present during July and August.  This suggests a May-July or early August spawning period on the southwest Florida coast.

Fecundity: One female, 2032 mm, contained ca. 12,202,000 eggs (1364).  Females probably spawn only once per season (579).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Unknown.  Eggs remain undescribed; eggs described by Breder (66) as tarpon eggs were misidentified (1367).

Larvae: Evidence suggests larval growth may be fairly rapid (198).  Development of larvae is divided into three stages: Stage I, a fully formed leptocephalus; Stage II, a period of marked shrinking during which the larva gradually loses its leptocephalus form; Stage III, begins with a second period of length increase and ends with the onset of the juvenile stage (749).

Larva1: Earliest stages unknown, maximum length attained 29.9 mm SL (1367).  Duration of stage: 2-3 mos. (659).  Essentially a period of length increase culminating in a fully formed leptocephalus larva (858).  Leptocephalus is characterized by a long, colorless, transparent, ribbon-like body with a small head and numerous sharp teeth (858).  Larva 5.7 mm NL collected with part of yolk sac remaining anteriorly in two parts: a spherical mass under the throat and a smaller portion just behind it (659).  Yolk sac lost at ca. 6 mm NL.  Notochord unflexed up to 10-11 mm NL; caudal rays begin to form at flexion.  Pectoral fin unrayed until metamorphosis; filaments appear on gill arches at about 15-16 mm SL; air bladder evident at 11.7 mm SL.  At 27 mm SL non-functional heart located posteroventrally to pectoral fin (366 1367).

Larva2: 27.3-13.0 mm SL (366).  Duration of stage 20-25 days in the laboratory (1367), but estimated to be 7-8 weeks in nature (858).  During this stage, the larva losses its leptocephalus characteristics and begins to take the juvenile form.  This stage is also characterized by a marked decrease in length (749).  From 27.3 mm to 25.0 mm SL body depth decreases (1367); at 17 mm SL head increases greatly in relative size (749); at 15 mm gut and nostrils well formed and gular plate developing (1367).  At 15 mm SL body becomes more opaque, dorsal and lateral parts silvery, coelomic cavity densely pigmented (1367).

Larva3: 12.6 to ca. 25 mm SL (1367).  A second period of length increase which terminates with the beginning of the juvenile stage (749).  Teeth on lower jaw throughout stage, developing on upper jaw from 13.9-14.1 mm SL.  At 13.8 mm SL, gas bladder enlarged anteriorly.  Chromatophores outline myomeres and are developed on body above midline at 15.9 mm SL.  Larvae translucent and pale emerald green at 18.1 SL (278).  Swim bladder bright silvery color due to guanine deposition and by 24.8 mm SL, larvae silvered over with guanine crystals (278).

Juvenile: Minimum size described 25.2 mm SL (749).  Growth rate during summer and early fall is ca. 30 mm per month (596).  Five marked juveniles (310-376 mm FL) exhibited a growth rate of 1.0 mm/day between August and October (1375).  Body opaque at 25.2 mm SL with pigment mostly above lateral line.  Scale formation begins along lateral line at ca. 29.7 mm SL (278).  At 194.1 mm SL, filamentous ray of dorsal grooved on underside; anal with scaly sheath and last ray produced; caudal scaly (749).  Juveniles become darker dorsally with age (1368).

Adult:  Reported to grow to approximately 400 mm SL during first year (1374). Mature at end of sixth or seventh winter (66 310).  Males smaller than females; 8 yr old males average 1280 mm FL and 8 yr old females average 1480 mm FL (579).  Females mature at ca. 1220 mm TL and weigh ca. 20 kg (66 310).  Males are mature by 1095 mm FL (579).  Cyr (1374) reported that the smallest mature female he collected was 1245 mm and approximately 13.8 years old; the smallest mature male was 1181 mm  (no age given).    Harrington (1368) presented the following length-weight relationship for tarpon 16.0 - 45.5 mm SL:
[eq]
                  W = 0.05514 (1.069^SL) - 0.15
[/eq]
where, W = weight in grams, and SL = standard length in mm.

Harrington (1368) also provided the following conversions between fork length (FL), standard length (SL), and total length (TL) in mm for tarpon 25 - 45 mm SL:
[eq]
                  FL = 1.1282(SL) - 1
                  TL = 1.3333(SL) - 2
[/eq]
Breder (66) provided the following length-weight relationship for adult tarpon in Florida:
[eq]
                  W = (9(10^-6)) (TL^3)
[/eq]
where W = weight in grams and TL = total length in mm.

Zale and Merrifield (858) derived the following relationship between total length and fork length for adults based on data presented by Moffett and Randall (1375):
[eq]
                  TL = 1.10(FL)
[/eq]
Maximum size reported as 2.4m (8 ft) and 136kg (300 lbs), with the world record gamefish reported as 129kg (283 lb)(788).  Scale rings have not been validated as annuli and should be used with extreme caution for age determination; maximum age based on scale rings reported as 16 years (1375).  Tarpon are long-lived and captive fish exceeding 50 years have been reported (1375).  Cyr (1374) estimated ages with various otolith measurements to around 50 yrs.

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body:
Strictly carnivorous with generalized food habits (515 749).  Stage I larvae do not feed but obtain nutrients directly from seawater by absorption (858); feeding begins in Stage II (1367).

Larvae and small juveniles: are primarily plankton feeders preying on copepods (cyclopoid and harpacticoid), mosquito larvae, and detritus (280 279 515 579 596 749 1375).  Large juveniles >45 mm SL begin gradually switching from copepods to small fish such as cyprinodonts, Membras martinica, Gambusia affinis, Mugil cephlus, and to caridean shrimp, ostracods, and insects (280 279 310 515 596 656 702).

Adults:  Feed both nocturnally and diurnally (749).  Predominately piscivorous with fish composing up to 95% of total food volume (279).  Tarpon prey on such fishes as mullet, marine catfish, pinfish, bream, sardines, needlefish, silversides, cutlass fish, and anchovies.  Shrimp are also an important diet component.  Other food items include: insects, blue crabs, and ctenophores (255 279 310 467 515 596 749 1364).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation: Predation of adults is limited to other large predators such as sharks, porpoises, and alligators, while the young fall victim to a variety of fish, other tarpon, and to piscivorous birds that include kingfishers, pelicans, and herons (310 579 596 749 750 1375).
Competition:  Possible competition may exist between tarpon and such frequently associated species as Centropomus undecimalis, Cynoscion nebulosus, and Elops saurus (596 749).  Tarpon are high trophic level carnivores preying mainly on fish (750).  Due to the large relative size of tarpon juveniles these fish undoubtedly shape the population structure of other species in habitats including wetland mosquito impoundments.

Parasites/Diseases:  Recorded parasites include: isopods (Cymothoa oestrum, Nerocila acuminata), copepods (Paralebion pearsei), trematodes (Bivescula tarponis, Lecithochirium microstomum), and parasites of the family Hemiuridae; remoras (Echeneis naucrates) are not parasitic, but have been found attached to large tarpon (749 858 1364).

sections.content:
Common Name: Tarpon
Scientific Name: Megalops atlanticus

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Elopiformes
	Family:  Elopidae


Other Common Names: tarpum(310 749 846); caffum(310 749); sabalo real, palika(310); sabalo (846 1364); silverfish(310 312 834 846 1364);  silver king(310 327 749); jewfish(310 312 1364); big scale(1364); grande ecaille(255 310 327 846 1364); grand ecoy(255 1364); sadina (1364); savalle, savanilla(846 1364); king fish(834)

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  No commercial value in United States where it is considered inedible (312 834 846 858 749 1364), but considered a delicacy in Panama, West Indies, and Africa, where it is sold on a small scale (66 310 749).  A commercial fishery exists in Colombia (791).  Caught mainly on hook and line, but also with dynamite in the southern Caribbean (791).  Flesh is rather fatty, but it is marketed fresh or salted (791 846).  Scales used in ornamental work and for the preparation of artificial pearls (312 791 834 846).

Recreational: Excellent game fish sought for sporting purposes throughout most of its range.  Well known for fighting ability and aerial acrobatics, it is commonly regarded as a prime inshore game fish (310 312 664 749 788 834 846 858 1364).  No size limit in Florida, but there is a 2 fish bag limit and a tarpon tag costing $50 is required to possess or kill.

Indicator:  Dieldrin, a chlorinated hydrocarbon used for mosquito control, has been shown to cause mortality to tarpon (750 1365 1366).  Tarpon are also considered natural monitors of toxic pollutants in inshore areas because of their freedom from reliance on dissolved oxygen for survival where, by contrast, oxygen depletion cannot be ruled out at the immediate cause of death of other species (278).

Ecological Role: Tarpon are high trophic level carnivores preying mainly on fish (750).  Due to the large relative size of tarpon juveniles these fish undoubtedly shape the population structure of other species in habitats including wetland mosquito impoundments.

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  In the western Atlantic from Nova Scotia, where it rarely occurs in the summer, to central Brazil and throughout the Gulf of Mexico and the West Indies (310 312 327 749 788 791 891 1037). Also reported at the Pacific terminus of the Panama Canal (749).  Occurrences from the Carolinas northward are sparse, and it appears only as a straggler north of the Carolinas (278 310 312 327 749 750 834).  Centers of abundance are the Gulf of Mexico, coastal Florida, and the West Indies (205 310 659 791 858).  In the eastern Atlantic from Ireland to the Congo with reports from Bermuda, the Azores, and the Formigas (738 749 750 791),  Center of abundance is from Senegal to the Congo (750).  Chief center of abundance is in the western Atlantic (750).

Within Study Area:  Found throughout Florida coastal waters (310 749 848 858 891).  Highly abundant on both the east and west coasts of Florida especially at Boca Grande and Captiva, western Florida; the waterways and rivers of the Thousand Islands, and the interior waterways of the Florida Keys (310 790).  Most abundant in the Tampa Bay area from spring through fall (664).

Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
Non-schooling but does form congregations while feeding (278 310 1037).  No information is available on eggs; early larval forms are pelagic and planktonic, while later larval stages, juveniles, and adults are pelagic and nektonic (231 659).  Some evidence of increased larval activity at night (735) while adults feed both day and night (749).

Spatial Strategy:  Larva1: (leptocephalus): Warm, western Atlantic epipelagic waters north of the equator with all recoveries occurring in the upper 100 m of water (749 1365) in euhaline salinities as far out as 240 km and to depths of 200 m (231 659 749 1372); also collected from inshore waters (198 1367).

Larva2:  (shrinking): Recorded from depths of <1 to 12 m in inshore waters (201 706 735). Collected in salt marshes, rivers, mangrove swamps, estuaries, and upper reaches of bays as far north as Cape Fear River, North Carolina (66 201 278 280 706 735 749) in mesohaline to euhaline waters (706 735 749).

Larva3: (growing): Found along beaches in lagoons, salt marshes, ponds, potholes, rivers and canals (280 310 366 749 1368); rarely collected as far north as North Carolina (1369).

Juvenile:  Smaller individuals found in shallow streams, lakes, marshes, lagoons, ponds, ditches, canals, rivers, estuaries, mangrove swamps, pools, and drainage ditches nearly or completely landlocked except for periods of extreme high water; also in headwaters of small freshwater streams (66 280 299 310 327 344 442 515 579 596 703 749 750).  Usually in dark colored brackish waters, stagnant or flowing (579 596 749) in depths of 15.2 to 152.4 cm (224 579 596 656 750).  Tarpon 305_487 mm common in headwaters of brackish and freshwater streams.  Movement to deeper rivers, canals, pools, lakes, and eventually to ocean occurs as individuals grow larger (310 750) being found in waters 0.9 to 2.5 m deep (224 255 596 702 750).  Juvenile tarpon are the largest predator utilizing wetland impoundments along the IRL (1272).

Adults: Primarily in coastal inshore waters, inlets, estuaries, and passes between islands, but also found in deeper rivers canals, streams, and lakes (66 310 327 395 749 750 788 791 848) in freshwater to marine environments (66 395 579 703 749 788 790 1365).

Movements and Migrations:  Observations suggest that tarpon larvae may move to offshore waters from spawning areas returning to inshore areas prior to metamorphosis (201 231 281 659).  As juvenile tarpon grow, they move from nursery grounds to deeper inshore waters and finally to the ocean (750).  Adult and large juvenile tarpon are capable of extensive movements, but patterns of coastal migration other than inshore-offshore movements in response to the cooling waters of winter are not evident (310 481 579), although some individuals apparently move northward along the Atlantic coast during the summer and are subsequently lost to the population (310).  Tarpon are most abundant inshore from April to November (69 320 668).  Assemblages of sexually maturing tarpon observed during spring and summer may by preparatory to an offshore spawning migration (481).

sections.heading: Substrate
sections.content: Juveniles and adults generally found over soft mud bottoms sometimes containing H2S, but also over sand, firm mud, sandy mud with no vegetation, peat (224 255 579 596 656 703 702 750), and occasionally on coral reefs (788).

sections.heading: Temperature
sections.content:
Eggs: No information

Larva1:  larvae occur only in warm oceanic waters ranging from 22.2 to 30.0 C (659 749).  They appear to prefer warmer waters (366).  Stage II larvae reported from 19.8  to 30.8 C (706 735).  Larva3: reported from 25.0 to 27.0 C (278).

Juveniles/Adults: Range and habitat essentially the same for both groups (749); they have been collected at temperatures ranging from 12.0 to 40.0 C (224 235 255 442 514 579 596 656 702 750 1375).  In Florida, juveniles have been collected at temperatures of 23.0 to 33.0 C at Naples and 17.0 to 37.0 C near Indian River (1374).  Loss of equilibrium or death observed from 9.5 to 18.2 C in the laboratory (344).  Mortality occurs in the wild at temperatures between 10.0 and 14.0 C following sudden cold snaps (596).  One dead specimen was found at Tampa Bay when water temperature was 13.0 C (664).  Resistance to cold might be greater during slow temperature falls (596 702).  Listed as one of the species killed by freezes at Sanibel Island, Florida (836 1068).

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content:
Eggs: No information

Larva1: Specimens taken from 28.5 to 39.0 ppt (198 659 749 1370 1371).  Possibly stenohaline, seeming to prefer high salinities as this stage is not generally found in low or fluctuating salinities, probably staying well offshore until the approach of metamorphosis (659).

Larva2/Larva3/Juvenile/Adult:  Euryhaline; collected at salinities ranging from 0.0 to 47 ppt, but seem to prefer salinities between 5.1 and 22.3 ppt (66 224 255 261 278 395 442 514 579 596 651 656 702 706 735 750).  Widely distributed in the freshwaters of south Florida where they are primarily restricted to deep water (790).  Found in freshwater canals throughout the Everglades, the Big Cypress Swamp and along both coasts (395). Also found in Lake Okeechobee (1313).

Dissolved oxygen: Tarpon are obligate air breathers (749) with metamorphosing larvae as small as 16 mm SL dying if kept from surfacing as do larger fish (278).  Juveniles may occupy areas of low DO as a way to avoid predators because many predators cannot tolerate anoxic waters (278 749).  Juvenile growth may be retarded by continued occupation of anoxic waters (1374).  Tarpon are able to breathe by means of rolling and gulping air which is held in a highly vascularized air bladder (514 750).  Their ability for aerial respiration allows them to survive in oxygen depleted waters with an oxygen content as low as 0.00 to 0.81 ppm (514).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: Sexes separate; probably external fertilization

Mating/Spawning: Unknown; apparently restricted to offshore waters such as east coast of Florida to Cape Hatteras, Florida Straits, west central Florida, southwestern Gulf of Mexico, Gulf Stream, and Caribbean Sea, or areas where currents can carry eggs offshore, possibly in shoal waters between coastal islands, or close to shore in salty or brackish water (66 198 281 310 366 659 750 1370).  Some populations may complete life cycle in fresh water (310).  Estimated spawning season is from May to September with near ripe females and milt ejecting males occurring in April and spent females occurring in July and August (66 198 310 366 579 659 750 1365).  Cyr (1374) examined reproductive condition of tarpon from Boca Grande, Tampa Bay and other south Florida areas. He found that the peak in reproductive development occurred in May and June with the greatest number of spent males and females present during July and August.  This suggests a May-July or early August spawning period on the southwest Florida coast.

Fecundity: One female, 2032 mm, contained ca. 12,202,000 eggs (1364).  Females probably spawn only once per season (579).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:  Unknown.  Eggs remain undescribed; eggs described by Breder (66) as tarpon eggs were misidentified (1367).

Larvae: Evidence suggests larval growth may be fairly rapid (198).  Development of larvae is divided into three stages: Stage I, a fully formed leptocephalus; Stage II, a period of marked shrinking during which the larva gradually loses its leptocephalus form; Stage III, begins with a second period of length increase and ends with the onset of the juvenile stage (749).

Larva1: Earliest stages unknown, maximum length attained 29.9 mm SL (1367).  Duration of stage: 2-3 mos. (659).  Essentially a period of length increase culminating in a fully formed leptocephalus larva (858).  Leptocephalus is characterized by a long, colorless, transparent, ribbon-like body with a small head and numerous sharp teeth (858).  Larva 5.7 mm NL collected with part of yolk sac remaining anteriorly in two parts: a spherical mass under the throat and a smaller portion just behind it (659).  Yolk sac lost at ca. 6 mm NL.  Notochord unflexed up to 10-11 mm NL; caudal rays begin to form at flexion.  Pectoral fin unrayed until metamorphosis; filaments appear on gill arches at about 15-16 mm SL; air bladder evident at 11.7 mm SL.  At 27 mm SL non-functional heart located posteroventrally to pectoral fin (366 1367).

Larva2: 27.3-13.0 mm SL (366).  Duration of stage 20-25 days in the laboratory (1367), but estimated to be 7-8 weeks in nature (858).  During this stage, the larva losses its leptocephalus characteristics and begins to take the juvenile form.  This stage is also characterized by a marked decrease in length (749).  From 27.3 mm to 25.0 mm SL body depth decreases (1367); at 17 mm SL head increases greatly in relative size (749); at 15 mm gut and nostrils well formed and gular plate developing (1367).  At 15 mm SL body becomes more opaque, dorsal and lateral parts silvery, coelomic cavity densely pigmented (1367).

Larva3: 12.6 to ca. 25 mm SL (1367).  A second period of length increase which terminates with the beginning of the juvenile stage (749).  Teeth on lower jaw throughout stage, developing on upper jaw from 13.9-14.1 mm SL.  At 13.8 mm SL, gas bladder enlarged anteriorly.  Chromatophores outline myomeres and are developed on body above midline at 15.9 mm SL.  Larvae translucent and pale emerald green at 18.1 SL (278).  Swim bladder bright silvery color due to guanine deposition and by 24.8 mm SL, larvae silvered over with guanine crystals (278).

Juvenile: Minimum size described 25.2 mm SL (749).  Growth rate during summer and early fall is ca. 30 mm per month (596).  Five marked juveniles (310-376 mm FL) exhibited a growth rate of 1.0 mm/day between August and October (1375).  Body opaque at 25.2 mm SL with pigment mostly above lateral line.  Scale formation begins along lateral line at ca. 29.7 mm SL (278).  At 194.1 mm SL, filamentous ray of dorsal grooved on underside; anal with scaly sheath and last ray produced; caudal scaly (749).  Juveniles become darker dorsally with age (1368).

Adult:  Reported to grow to approximately 400 mm SL during first year (1374). Mature at end of sixth or seventh winter (66 310).  Males smaller than females; 8 yr old males average 1280 mm FL and 8 yr old females average 1480 mm FL (579).  Females mature at ca. 1220 mm TL and weigh ca. 20 kg (66 310).  Males are mature by 1095 mm FL (579).  Cyr (1374) reported that the smallest mature female he collected was 1245 mm and approximately 13.8 years old; the smallest mature male was 1181 mm  (no age given).    Harrington (1368) presented the following length-weight relationship for tarpon 16.0 - 45.5 mm SL:
[eq]
                  W = 0.05514 (1.069^SL) - 0.15
[/eq]
where, W = weight in grams, and SL = standard length in mm.

Harrington (1368) also provided the following conversions between fork length (FL), standard length (SL), and total length (TL) in mm for tarpon 25 - 45 mm SL:
[eq]
                  FL = 1.1282(SL) - 1
                  TL = 1.3333(SL) - 2
[/eq]
Breder (66) provided the following length-weight relationship for adult tarpon in Florida:
[eq]
                  W = (9(10^-6)) (TL^3)
[/eq]
where W = weight in grams and TL = total length in mm.

Zale and Merrifield (858) derived the following relationship between total length and fork length for adults based on data presented by Moffett and Randall (1375):
[eq]
                  TL = 1.10(FL)
[/eq]
Maximum size reported as 2.4m (8 ft) and 136kg (300 lbs), with the world record gamefish reported as 129kg (283 lb)(788).  Scale rings have not been validated as annuli and should be used with extreme caution for age determination; maximum age based on scale rings reported as 16 years (1375).  Tarpon are long-lived and captive fish exceeding 50 years have been reported (1375).  Cyr (1374) estimated ages with various otolith measurements to around 50 yrs.

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content:
Strictly carnivorous with generalized food habits (515 749).  Stage I larvae do not feed but obtain nutrients directly from seawater by absorption (858); feeding begins in Stage II (1367).

Larvae and small juveniles: are primarily plankton feeders preying on copepods (cyclopoid and harpacticoid), mosquito larvae, and detritus (280 279 515 579 596 749 1375).  Large juveniles >45 mm SL begin gradually switching from copepods to small fish such as cyprinodonts, Membras martinica, Gambusia affinis, Mugil cephlus, and to caridean shrimp, ostracods, and insects (280 279 310 515 596 656 702).

Adults:  Feed both nocturnally and diurnally (749).  Predominately piscivorous with fish composing up to 95% of total food volume (279).  Tarpon prey on such fishes as mullet, marine catfish, pinfish, bream, sardines, needlefish, silversides, cutlass fish, and anchovies.  Shrimp are also an important diet component.  Other food items include: insects, blue crabs, and ctenophores (255 279 310 467 515 596 749 1364).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Predation: Predation of adults is limited to other large predators such as sharks, porpoises, and alligators, while the young fall victim to a variety of fish, other tarpon, and to piscivorous birds that include kingfishers, pelicans, and herons (310 579 596 749 750 1375).
Competition:  Possible competition may exist between tarpon and such frequently associated species as Centropomus undecimalis, Cynoscion nebulosus, and Elops saurus (596 749).  Tarpon are high trophic level carnivores preying mainly on fish (750).  Due to the large relative size of tarpon juveniles these fish undoubtedly shape the population structure of other species in habitats including wetland mosquito impoundments.

Parasites/Diseases:  Recorded parasites include: isopods (Cymothoa oestrum, Nerocila acuminata), copepods (Paralebion pearsei), trematodes (Bivescula tarponis, Lecithochirium microstomum), and parasites of the family Hemiuridae; remoras (Echeneis naucrates) are not parasitic, but have been found attached to large tarpon (749 858 1364).
